reading.rtitle: Outline Specification -- Residential Tower, Vila Mariana
paras: This outline specification goes with drawing set Revision C for a twelve-story residential building on a two-level basement in Vila Mariana, São Paulo. It describes the structure, the main materials and the rules for using the drawings on site. Where a drawing and this specification do not agree, the contractor must flag the discrepancy and submit an RFI to the designer before the work starts. Nobody decides on site.

The building has a reinforced-concrete frame. The typical floor slabs are 20-centimeter flat slabs, except on the ground floor, where a 40-centimeter transfer slab carries the columns of the tower above the basement. The walls shown in red on the floor plans are load-bearing walls: they must not be opened, cut or moved without the written approval of the structural engineer. All dimensions are in millimeters unless noted otherwise, and drawings marked N.T.S. are not to scale. Never measure them with a ruler.

Every drawing has its revision letter in the title block. Before a crew starts work in any area, the foreman must cross-reference the floor plan, the elevation and the cross-section of that area and confirm that all three show the latest revision. Old drawings must be removed from the site office on the day a new revision arrives. At the end of the work, the contractor delivers a full set of as-built drawings that show what was actually built, including every change approved during construction.

listenings.text: I am the project architect, and I want to tell you about the most expensive mistake I see on construction sites. It is not a design mistake. It is an old drawing. Somebody prints Revision B, pins it to the wall of the site office, and three weeks later the crew is still building from it, although Revision C changed the stair and a two-meter opening on the fourth floor. Nobody was careless. The new drawing simply never reached the person with the tape measure. So my rule is very simple. When a new revision arrives, the old drawings leave the site office the same day. And before any crew starts work, the foreman checks the revision letter in the title block. It takes thirty seconds.

On my second project as a site engineer, I was checking the drawings for a six-story office building, and I noticed something strange. The architectural plan showed a large opening in a wall on the ground floor, but on the structural drawings, the same wall was a load-bearing wall. My foreman wanted to start cutting on Monday. Instead, I flagged the discrepancy and sent an RFI to the structural engineer. He answered in two days. The architect had moved the opening in the last revision, and nobody had told the structure team. If we had cut that wall, we would have lost weeks, and maybe much more. Since then, I cross-reference every drawing before a crew touches anything.
